theme: The Last Supper; teaching on greatness; Gethsemane
readingInstruction: Read Luke 22:1-46. The plot, the betrayal bargain, the Last Supper, the argument about greatness, Peter’s warning, and Gethsemane. Read slowly, and let the Supper words settle.
settingTheScene: It is the week of Passover. The religious leaders are looking for a way to put Jesus to death without upsetting the people. Satan enters Judas. In an upper room, Jesus eats the Passover with his disciples and gives the meal a new meaning. Then he leads them to the Mount of Olives to pray, as was his custom. Luke’s account is among the most intimate in the Gospels.
observation: “Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve” (22:3).
“I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (22:15).
“This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (22:19).
“This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (22:20).
“But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves” (22:26).
“But I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (22:32).
“Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (22:42).
“Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation” (22:46).
interpretation:
Luke moves quickly. The leaders are afraid of the people, and Satan enters Judas, who agrees to betray Jesus for money. Meanwhile Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover meal.

At the table, Jesus says, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” He takes bread and says, “This is my body, given for you,” and after supper takes the cup and says, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.” This is the heart of the chapter. The Passover remembered the lamb whose blood spared Israel in Egypt. Now Jesus says that his body and blood will be given for his people. He is the Lamb, and the new covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 is being inaugurated by his death. Christians have disagreed about exactly how Christ is present in the Supper, but all agree that he commanded the church to keep it, and that it proclaims his death until he comes.

At the table, Jesus names his betrayer, and the disciples argue about which of them is the greatest. It is one of the saddest scenes in the Gospels. Jesus answers with a reversal: the kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, but “not so with you.” The greatest must be as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. “I am among you as the one who serves.” Then he promises that they will sit on thrones, a covenant of kingdom from his Father.

He turns to Peter: “Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail.” Notice that Jesus does not say he will keep Peter from falling. He says he has prayed that his faith will not fail, and that Peter will turn again and strengthen his brothers. Jesus foretells Peter’s denial, and Peter swears he will never deny him.

On the Mount of Olives, Jesus withdraws a stone’s throw and prays: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” An angel strengthens him. Then in agony he prays more earnestly. (Some early manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44, but the scene they describe fits the whole.) He finds the disciples sleeping from sorrow. “Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” The Son does what Adam did not: he submits to the will of the Father.
connection: Exodus 12 is the Passover. Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises the new covenant. Isaiah 53:12 says he poured out his soul to death. 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 is Paul’s account of the Supper. Hebrews 5:7-8 describes the prayers and cries of Jesus. Mark 10:42-45 is the parallel on servant leadership. John 13:1-17 shows Jesus washing the disciples’ feet. 1 Peter 5:8 warns that the devil prowls like a roaring lion.
application:
When you receive the Lord’s Supper, think about each word: broken for you, poured out for you.

Practice the service of the one who serves. Do something humble for someone today, unseen if possible.

Pray Jesus’ prayer in your hardest decision: “Not my will, but yours.”
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for the Passover he earnestly desired to eat with his disciples.
Tell him about the cup you are afraid to drink, and pray, “Not my will but yours.”
Ask him to help you stay awake and pray.
